Consider the matrices above. Given that $A = P J P^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/a985e5861e7360654b98ca334fac6d55f435e271dcc52b313e350f74a4c755c5.png)
worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ consists of one Jordan block $J = J_2(1).$ 

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(1) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda=1.$ 

Now, computing $A-1I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $\mathbf x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/624e955f479c8193ff32f3bebf0decb7b1d6b45fb5ec44db637d956e3a8d1ea7.png)
and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/0855b40d83950bcdfeda8447e74187f498fbfe73050e1e8fd7755a1ad4b1dbd0.png)

Therefore, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.
